passage:
"Not so close, Harish," said Parul, laughing, at the bus stop in Surat. Harish, five, leaned right into her face to show a beetle in his palm.
"It's big!"
"It is! But let's take one step back so I can see it. About an arm's length." She stretched out an arm. Harish stepped back until his fingers nearly touched it.
"Like that?"
"Perfect. Grandma gets a closer look though, right?"
"Yes, Grandma gets a hug." He grinned, and went to find the beetle a leaf.

qa.q: What was in Harish's palm?
qa.a: There was a big beetle in his palm.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling as he leaned into Parul's face?
qa.a: He was probably excited and eager to share his discovery, which is why he got so close. He probably wasn't trying to bother her.

qa.q: What made Parul's way of teaching personal space work?
qa.a: She explained it kindly with an arm's length and a clear example, and said some people such as Grandma can stand closer.

qa.q: How might Parul feel when Harish leans right into her face?
qa.a: She may feel a little crowded, though she stays friendly and gives him a clear guide.

grounding: A child learns that arm's length is a fair distance for many talks and that family may stand closer.

passage: Class note by Mridul, Reception teacher in Jaipur. Sumit, five, stands very close to friends when he speaks, so close that Aarav shrinks back. Today I knelt beside Sumit and said, "Let's find the right distance. Hold out your arm. That's the space where we usually talk." Then I asked him to practise with me. He stepped back, and beamed. Later, in a crowded queue, another child, Neel, froze and clutched his bag. I've taught the class to say, "Please give me space." Neel used it, and children moved back.

qa.q: How did Mridul teach Sumit the right distance?
qa.a: Mridul asked Sumit to hold out his arm and showed him that this is the space where we usually talk.

qa.q: What might Neel have been feeling when he froze in the crowded queue?
qa.a: He was probably uncomfortable at being crowded, since he clutched his bag. He might also have been unsure how to speak up.

qa.q: What could Mridul do to keep helping both children?
qa.a: Mridul can keep practising the arm's length and the sentence "Please give me space" with the whole class.

qa.q: How might Aarav feel when Sumit stands too close?
qa.a: Aarav may feel uncomfortable and want to move away, so the clear words help Aarav too.

grounding: A child learns arm's length is a fair distance, and children who crowd or freeze need gentle coaching and clear words.

passage: At the dairy counter in the village, Uday stood so close to Baljeet Singh that his nose nearly touched the counter's edge by the man's elbow. Baljeet laughed and stepped back. “Arre, too close, little one!” He stretched out his arm. “See? This much space for talking. With your amma you can stand close, but with shopkeepers, one arm.” Uday stretched his arm out too and stepped back till his fingers touched the counter. “Like this?” “Perfect. Now, how much milk?”

qa.q: What did Baljeet Singh stretch out to show the space?
qa.a: His arm.

qa.q: What might Uday have been thinking when he stood so close?
qa.a: He was probably curious and excited, not aware that standing so close could make someone uncomfortable. He wanted to be part of the talk.

qa.q: What made Baljeet's coaching work?
qa.a: He used a clear, friendly demonstration with his arm and simple words, and explained that family can be closer.

qa.q: How might Uday's amma see this lesson?
qa.a: She might be pleased that he learned arm's length kindly, and that he knows he can still be close to her.

grounding: A child crowds a shopkeeper and learns kindly that an arm's length is a fair distance, while family may stand closer.

passage: At circle time in the kindergarten in Madrid, the children crowded around Elif to see her new shoes. She froze, arms tight at her sides, and her lip wobbled. Valentina, the teacher, noticed. “Everyone, let's make our circle bigger. Stretch your arms out and take one step back.” The children did. Then Valentina crouched by Elif. “When it's too crowded, you can say, ‘Space, please.’” Elif nodded. She tried it the next time a friend leaned in, and the friend stepped back.

qa.q: What did the children crowd around Elif to see?
qa.a: Her new shoes.

qa.q: What did Elif's freezing and wobbling lip suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and uncomfortable with so many children close. She might also have felt shy about being the centre of attention.

qa.q: What small step did Valentina give Elif?
qa.a: She gave her the words “Space, please” to use when it is too crowded.

qa.q: How might the other children see Elif's freezing?
qa.a: They were excited about the shoes and probably didn't notice she was uncomfortable until the teacher spoke.

grounding: A child freezes when crowded, and her teacher coaches the group about arm's length and gives her clear words.

passage: Trisha loved talking to Devika, the art helper at the community centre. But she stood right up against Devika's knees, face tipped up, talking into her chin. Devika gently held Trisha's shoulders and moved her back a little. “I love hearing about your painting. Let's talk with this much space.” She held out her arm. Trisha stepped back. “Why?” “Some people feel squished when someone is very close. With your mum you can sit on her lap.” Trisha grinned. “With you, one arm.”

qa.q: Who was Devika at the community centre?
qa.a: The art helper.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling as she stood right up close?
qa.a: She was excited and fond of Devika, eager to share her painting, and didn't realise the closeness might feel squished.

qa.q: What would you advise an adult coaching a child about personal space?
qa.a: Stay warm, show the distance with an arm, and explain simply that family can be closer, as Devika did.

qa.q: How might Devika have felt with Trisha right against her knees?
qa.a: She probably felt a bit squished but also liked Trisha's affection, so she moved her back gently.

grounding: A child crowds a helper while talking and is coached gently about arm's length and closer distance with family.

passage:
I'm Suraj, and I sit next to Gautam in class. Gautam always stands really close when he talks, right up at your nose. Yesterday he told me about his new shoes so close I stepped back into the wall.

Teacher saw. She called us both over. "Let's try this. Stretch out your arm, Gautam. That's a good space for talking to friends."

Gautam stretched his arm, grinned, and stepped back. It looked a bit strange at first.

At home time his Nani squeezed him in a big hug, and he didn't step back at all.

qa.q: What did Gautam tell Suraj about?
qa.a: His new shoes.

qa.q: What might Gautam be feeling when he stands so close?
qa.a: He is probably excited and eager to share, not trying to crowd anyone; his grin when Teacher coached him suggests he felt fine about learning the new rule, maybe a little surprised.

qa.q: How did Teacher coach Gautam?
qa.a: She gave him a clear, simple measure, stretching out his arm, instead of scolding him, so he knew what a comfortable distance looks like.

qa.q: How does the close talking affect Suraj?
qa.a: It makes Suraj uncomfortable enough to step back into the wall, even though Gautam is only chatting.

grounding: It shows a child learning that about an arm's length suits talking with friends while family can come closer, with gentle coaching.
